common_misconceptions.topic: Greek and Roman gods are equivalent but not identical
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the Greek and Roman gods as simply the same gods with two names. They share roles (Zeus/Jupiter, Hera/Juno, Poseidon/Neptune, Athena/Minerva, Aphrodite/Venus) but Roman religion adapted and reframed them, and the cultural emphasis differs (Roman religion is more civic, ritual and state-focused; Greek myth is richer in narrative). Exam answers must use the correct name for the culture being discussed and can gain marks for informed Greek-Roman comparison.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), Myth and Religion, Gods.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat foundation myths and the Trojan War as straightforward history. Myths (Romulus and Remus, Athena and Poseidon, the events of the Odyssey) are stories that carried meaning — explaining the world, legitimising power, expressing values — not factual records. At the same time, the Mycenaean material culture IS archaeological evidence. Students must distinguish the world OF the poems (mythic) from the historical Mycenaean world (archaeological), a distinction the Homeric World component is built around.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), The Homeric World, historical and cultural background.

common_misconceptions.topic: Use the prescribed sources as evidence
common_misconceptions.misconception: Classical Civilisation is source-based. Students lose marks by writing general knowledge without referring to the prescribed literary sources (the Homeric Hymns, the Odyssey, Livy) and visual/material sources (the Lion Gate, the Mask of Agamemnon, the Parthenon, named vases and reliefs). Top answers name and use specific sources as evidence and, where relevant, discuss how literary and material sources present things differently.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), Knowledge, Understanding and Skills.

common_misconceptions.topic: Xenia is a two-way obligation, not just kindness
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students reduce xenia (guest-friendship) to 'being nice to guests'. It is a sacred, reciprocal obligation protected by Zeus: hosts must welcome, feed and gift the stranger before asking who they are; guests must not abuse hospitality. The Odyssey is structured around good hosts (the Phaeacians) and bad hosts/guests (Polyphemus, the suitors). Understanding xenia as a moral and religious system is central to analysing the poem.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), The Homeric World, society and values.

common_misconceptions.topic: The 'Mask of Agamemnon' is not really Agamemnon
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the gold death mask is genuinely the face of Agamemnon. Schliemann named it so, but it dates to around the 16th century BC, centuries before any historical Trojan War would have occurred. It is a Mycenaean royal funerary mask from Shaft Grave V, Grave Circle A — evidence of Mycenaean wealth and burial custom, not a portrait of the Homeric king. Precision about what material sources actually are wins marks.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), The Homeric World, burial customs.

common_misconceptions.topic: The architectural orders are specific and identifiable
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. Doric is plain with a simple capital (the Parthenon, the Temple of Zeus at Olympia); Ionic has scroll-like volutes; Corinthian has elaborate acanthus-leaf capitals. Being able to identify the order and link it to named temples is examinable knowledge for the Temples topic.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), Myth and Religion, Temples.

common_misconceptions.topic: Animal sacrifice was the central act of worship, not a barbaric oddity
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students react to sacrifice as strange or cruel rather than understanding its function. Sacrifice was the central, normal act of Greek and Roman worship — a shared meal with the gods, performed at the altar outside the temple, that maintained the reciprocal relationship between humans and gods (do ut des, 'I give so that you may give'). The ritual structure (procession, prayer, the killing, burning the gods' portion, feasting on the rest) is examinable.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), Myth and Religion, religion in everyday life.

common_misconceptions.topic: Heracles is Greek; Hercules is the Roman form
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix the names. Heracles is the Greek hero; Hercules is the Roman version of the same figure. He matters as the UNIVERSAL hero — important to both cultures — celebrated for his strength, his twelve labours, his suffering and his eventual apotheosis (becoming a god). Use the right form of the name for the culture in question.
common_misconceptions.source: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation specification (J199), Myth and Religion, The Universal Hero.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Name / Identify: Give the single required name or term (a god, a hero, a site, an artefact). One accurate word or name is enough; do not write a sentence.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State / Give: Give two distinct points, or one named item plus a detail. For 'give two of the labours of Heracles', two correct named labours score full marks.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Describe: Give an account with relevant detail. For a source or artefact, describe what is actually shown (figures, scene, materials) rather than interpreting it.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Give reasons, linked to evidence. Use 'because' and refer to a named source or example. Two developed reasons usually reach the top.
student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — Source Analysis: Analyse the prescribed source given. Refer closely to specific details IN the source (what is depicted, what is said) and use them to support a point. Do not just describe — connect the detail to the question. Balance literary and visual/material evidence where the question allows.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Explain (Extended Response): A developed explanation using named sources and examples. Structure two or three points, each supported with specific evidence from the prescribed material.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Essay (Extended Response): The extended essay rewards a clear argument supported by a RANGE of named sources (literary AND material where relevant), with analysis and a supported judgement. Candidates who narrate the myth or describe sources without arguing a case cap mid-band. Reach a conclusion that answers the question.
student_errors_by_question_type.10 marks — Essay (Extended Response): The highest-tariff essay. Sustain a balanced argument across several well-chosen sources, weigh different interpretations, and reach a justified judgement. Use precise classical detail (named gods, sites, artefacts, episodes). The judgement must be present and argued, not merely implied.

topic_weighting_notes: OCR GCSE Classical Civilisation (J199) is assessed by two equally-weighted written papers, each 50% of the qualification: Component Group 1 Thematic Study (here Myth and Religion, J199/11) and Component Group 2 Literature and Culture (here The Homeric World, J199/21). There is no coursework, so the whole specification is examined and revisable. (Source: OCR specification J199, section 2.)

Assessment objectives: AO1 (demonstrate knowledge and understanding of classical sources and the social/historical/cultural context), AO2 (analyse, interpret and evaluate classical sources and form judgements). The extended essays carry the heaviest AO2 weighting — argument and judgement, not just recall, decide the top grades. (Source: OCR specification J199, assessment objectives.)

Both components are SOURCE-LED. Myth and Religion uses prescribed literary sources (e.g. the Homeric Hymns, Livy) and prescribed visual/material sources (named temples, sculptures, vases). The Homeric World uses the Odyssey (prescribed books 9, 10, 19, 21, 22) plus prescribed material sources from Mycenae and Tiryns. Content must teach students to name and use these sources, not just the general story.

The Homeric World deliberately pairs ARCHAEOLOGY (the historical Mycenaean world — sites, palaces, graves, material culture) with LITERATURE (the Odyssey). Students must handle both and understand the relationship and the differences between the world the poems describe and the archaeological evidence.
Greek-Roman comparison is explicitly required in Myth and Religion: students compare Greek and Roman gods, temples, festivals and customs, and consider how cultural context shapes each.
current_spec_changes: OCR specification J199 is at version 1.5 (2024). The prescribed sources are fixed by the specification and the OCR source booklets (free to download). Content should teach the prescribed sources but must use original explanation and public-domain texts — do not reproduce the wording of OCR's source booklets.

All prescribed literary sources (Homer, the Homeric Hymns, Livy) are ancient and in the public domain; teach them in original prose and accurate summary. Prescribed visual/material sources (the Lion Gate, the Mask of Agamemnon, the Parthenon sculptures, named vases) are described and analysed but not reproduced as images in free-tier lessons.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — Classical Civilisation has a precise vocabulary that must be taught explicitly: the names and Greek/Roman forms of gods, technical terms (megaron, cella, xenia, kleos, nostos, apotheosis, Cyclopean, tholos, the architectural orders), and the names of sites and sources. Teach a tight glossary per lesson and drill it; spelling variations are accepted but the correct concept is not. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.)

Source-based discipline — model how to move from a source detail to a point. For a visual source: 'the Lion Gate shows two lions flanking a central column above the gate -> this projects the power and wealth of Mycenae -> it also suggests a religious or royal symbol'. For a literary source: quote or paraphrase a specific moment in the Odyssey and link it to the question. Students do not do this automatically. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance.)

Dual coding for material culture — the citadel of Mycenae, the megaron plan, the architectural orders, the layout of a temple, and the shaft graves are all visual. Even without images in the lesson, describe the visual layout precisely in words and have students reproduce a labelled mental plan. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Compare and contrast as a thinking routine — the specification repeatedly asks for Greek vs Roman comparison and for the relationship between the mythic world and the archaeological evidence. Build explicit comparison tables (Greek god vs Roman god; the world of the Odyssey vs Mycenaean archaeology) into revision. (Source: EEF Cognitive Science Approaches in the Classroom.)

Narrative is a strength to harness, not just indulge — students love the myths and the Odyssey's adventures. Use the story as the hook, then push beyond narration to ANALYSIS (why does this myth matter? what does this source show? what is the argument?), because the marks, especially in the essays, are for argument and use of evidence, not retelling. (Source: EEF Metacognition guidance; OCR examiner reports on over-narration.)

Evaluation scaffolds for the essays — teach a repeatable approach to the 8- and 10-mark essays: take a clear position, support it with a range of NAMED sources (literary and material), consider an alternative view, and reach a justified judgement. Students who carry this structure reliably reach the top band. (Source: EEF guidance on extended writing.)

gaps: This build covers the two most widely-taught options of OCR J199: Myth and Religion (Thematic Study) and The Homeric World (Literature and Culture). The alternative options (War and Warfare; Roman City Life) are not covered in this build and could be added later as further units.

Prescribed visual/material sources (the Lion Gate, the Mask of Agamemnon, the Parthenon sculptures, named vases and temples) are described and analysed in prose but not reproduced as images in free-tier lessons. Students should view the images in the OCR source booklets or a museum/online collection alongside these lessons.
There is no non-exam assessment in GCSE Classical Civilisation — the whole specification is examined across the two written papers, so every topic is covered by this revision build.
